question: Which are the better knowers of yoga — the devotees who, ever joined, worship Kṛṣṇa, or those who worship 'the imperishable, the unmanifest' (BhG 12.1)? And what is 'the imperishable, the unmanifest'?

sides.position: The 'imperishable unmanifest' is the attributeless brahman. Its worshippers, renunciant knowers, reach the Lord because the knower is the Lord's very self (7.18); calling the devotees of the Lord 'most joined' (12.2) does not place them above these knowers. The path of the unmanifest is harder for those who identify with the body (12.5), which is why graded means are taught to the others (12.8–11); the marks of 12.13–19 describe the worshippers of the imperishable.
arguments: 'they too reach me alone' (12.4) read with 7.18 ('the knower is my very self')
the hardship of 12.5 is due to identification with the body

sides.position: The 'imperishable unmanifest' is the individual self in its own nature, not perceptible to the senses. Those who meditate on it reach a self of the same kind as the Lord, slowly and with hardship; those who meditate on the Lord himself are superior, reach him swiftly and are lifted by him (12.2, 12.6–7).
arguments: the contrast of greater hardship (12.5) with swift deliverance (12.7)

notes: The text's own answer (12.2–5): those who fix manas on the Lord and worship him with supreme faith are held 'most joined'; the worshippers of the imperishable also reach him, but with greater hardship for the embodied. The two commentarial positions are recorded from the extractor's knowledge of the bhāṣyas, not from their texts; they need checking against src:gita-bhasya-sankara and src:gita-bhasya-ramanuja.
